title: Boss: the reports that lied
summary: Three scheduled reports run without an error and print the wrong answer. Find out why from what they print, and fix each one.

steps.title: Ticket OPS-2291
body: *"The morning disk report says nothing is big, the sales mail ranks Northwind above Contoso, and finance says the
revenue CSV is full of nonsense. Nothing failed in the scheduler. Please look before Monday."*
Three scripts in `~/scripts`, three quiet bugs. Run each one, read what it prints, compare it with the data, fix it.
None of them throws an error: that is the point. Every check runs your fixed script for real.

steps.title: Nothing is big?
prompt: `pwsh -File ~/scripts/big-files.ps1` says `0 files over 5 MB`, but `~/data` clearly has bigger files
1. Find and fix the bug, so it reports the 4 files over 5 MB, biggest first.
2. Make the next bug like this one impossible to miss: add `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest` right **after** the
`param(...)` line (a `param` block must stay the first statement of a script).

checks.name: it reports 4 files over 5 MB
checks.fail: The first line should be `4 files over 5 MB`.

checks.name: biggest first
checks.fail: The second line should be the biggest file, `db-2026-11-15.bak`.

checks.name: strict mode is on, after param()
checks.fail: Add `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest` on a line after `param(...)`.

checks.name: strict mode now catches a misspelt property
checks.cmd: sed 's/\$_\.Length -gt/$_.Lenght -gt/' ~/scripts/big-files.ps1 > /tmp/typo.ps1; pwsh -NoProfile -File /tmp/typo.ps1 2>&1 | grep -qi 'cannot be found on this object'
checks.fail: With strict mode on, a misspelt property such as `$_.Lenght` must raise an error instead of quietly being `$null`.

hints: Read the `Where-Object` line letter by letter. What does PowerShell do when you ask an object for a property it does not have?
`$_.Lenght` does not exist, so it is `$null`, and `$null -gt 5MB` is false for every file. Fix the spelling to `Length`.

One way to edit: `$t = Get-Content ~/scripts/big-files.ps1 -Raw`, then `$t -replace 'Lenght', 'Length' -replace '(?m)^(param\(.*\))$', ('$1' + "`nSet-StrictMode -Version Latest")`, and `Set-Content` it back with `-NoNewline`. Or `nano ~/scripts/big-files.ps1`.
explain: By default PowerShell returns `$null` for a property that does not exist, and `$null` compares as false. One typo
and a report says "nothing to do" for months. `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest` turns that (and reading an unset
variable, and calling a function like a method) into errors. Put it at the top of every script you schedule.

steps.title: Northwind above Contoso?
prompt: `pwsh -File ~/scripts/top-customers.ps1` is meant to print the three customers with the **most revenue**. Compare its
output with `Import-Csv ~/data/sales.csv`. Fix the script so it prints, in this order:

checks.name: the top three by revenue, in order
checks.fail: The script should print the three biggest customers by revenue, biggest first.

hints: Strings sort character by character, so `'9500'` beats `'104000'`. Sort by a number instead.
steps.explain: Anything read from text (CSV, `Get-Content`, environment variables, most query strings) is a string until you convert it. A cleaner fix for a real report converts once, right after reading: `Import-Csv ... | Select-Object Customer, @{ n = 'Revenue'; e = { [decimal]$_.Revenue } }`, so every later step gets numbers.

steps.title: A CSV full of nonsense
prompt: Finance opens `~/reports/revenue.csv` from `~/scripts/export-report.ps1` and sees columns like
Fix the script so the CSV has exactly the columns **`Customer`** and **`Revenue`**, one row per customer.

checks.name: revenue.csv has Customer and Revenue for every customer
cmd: if not os.path.exists(p): sys.exit('the script did not write ~/reports/revenue.csv')
if cols != ['Customer', 'Revenue']: sys.exit(f'columns are {cols[:4]}, expected Customer, Revenue')
got = [(r['Customer'], r['Revenue']) for r in rows]
if sorted(got) != sorted(want): sys.exit(f'rows {got} do not match the sales data')
checks.fail: The CSV should have the header `Customer,Revenue` and one row per customer from `~/data/sales.csv`.

hints: Look at what `Format-Table` outputs: `Import-Csv ~/data/sales.csv | Format-Table Customer, Revenue | Get-Member`.
`Format-Table` emits formatting objects for the screen. `Export-Csv` faithfully wrote *their* properties.
solution: Import-Csv ~/data/sales.csv | Format-Table Customer, Revenue | Get-Member | Select-Object -First 3
explain: The rule from the toolkit, learned the expensive way: `Format-*` only at the very end, for eyes. `Select-Object` picks
properties and keeps real objects that any next command (`Export-Csv`, `ConvertTo-Json`, `Where-Object`) understands.
The scheduler showed success because nothing failed: always look at a script's *output* once, not only its exit code.
